strengths: Comprehensive and well-executed foundation model for volumetric CT: SPECTRE combines an adapted DINOv3-style SSL stage (DINO + iBOT + KoLeo) with a SigLIP-based vision-language stage over a large (~230K series) corpus built exclusively from openly available datasets, which is a meaningful contribution given the field's reliance on private data.

Evaluation is unusually thorough and protocol-faithful: the standardized TumorImagingBench kNN protocol of Pai et al. is applied uniformly across 11 CT foundation models with 95% confidence intervals (Fig. 3); segmentation is evaluated as a drop-in nnU-Net encoder replacement across four established benchmarks; retrieval is evaluated on CT-RATE and Merlin with the original protocols.

Results are genuinely competitive: best on 4/6 frozen-embedding biomarker benchmarks (with narrow CIs on LUNA16, DLCS, NSCLC-Radiomics), best among transformer-based segmentation models on AMOS-CT, KiTS23, LiTS, WORD, and substantially improved zero-shot retrieval over CT-CLIP (17.5 vs 2.9 R@5) and over Merlin on Impressions retrieval.

The paper is honest about weaknesses: it acknowledges thoracic-skewed pretraining data, reduced segmentation fidelity at 1/4-resolution predictions, and explicitly avoids optimism bias by excluding the fold used for tuning (KiTS23 fold-0) from reported cross-validation.

Reproducibility is strong: full training code, recipes, model weights, dataset curation details, hyperparameters (Tab. 5), and architecture specs (Tab. 6) are released, plus ablations on optimizer, deep supervision, crop size, and SSL vs VLA initialization (Tab. 7).
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the contribution is largely a careful assembly of existing techniques (DINOv3-style distillation, SigLIP, 3D RoPE, EoMT-style encoder-only segmentation) adapted to 3D CT. The two-stage local/global ViT design (24-layer ViT_l + only 4-layer ViT_g) is plausible but not ablated against simpler alternatives (e.g., plain ViT with global attention, or joint vs. staged SSL+VLA training), so the architectural claims about handling 'extreme token scaling' are asserted rather than demonstrated.

Not all empirical claims are fully supported: the assertion that SigLIP is preferable for 'noisy and many-to-many' clinical image-text pairs is not backed by an ablation against CLIP-style InfoNCE; the 4/6 benchmark result is solid but the model falls behind Merlin on structured Findings retrieval and below nnU-Net ResEnc L on LiTS/WORD segmentation, so 'consistently outperforms prior CT foundation models' (abstract) is somewhat overstated relative to the mixed picture.

Biomarker evaluation relies solely on frozen kNN; no linear-probe or fine-tuned results are reported for the classification tasks, and two of the six datasets (NSCLC-Radiogenomics, n=133; C4KC-KiTS, n=134) are small enough that, as the authors themselves note, all models show large CIs and low scores — limiting the strength of conclusions on prognostic transfer.

Some presentation issues: the 'effective compression factor' of 2048/1080 ≈ 1.8962 is dimensionally opaque; Fig. 1 (radar plot) is a poor medium for precise comparison though mitigated by Fig. 3; several baselines (WaveFormer, Primus on AMOS-CT) have missing entries; the LLM-based report paraphrasing pipeline (Gemini 2 Flash) introduces a potentially unquantified source of supervision noise that is neither validated nor ablated.

Discussion of scaling behavior is thin for a paper titled 'Scaling...': only a single model configuration is trained and evaluated; no experiments on model/data size scaling to support the scalability claims, and the Gram-loss omission from DINOv3 is justified only by argument.

strengths: Comprehensive, standardized evaluation: the paper applies the TumorImagingBench protocol (Pai et al.) uniformly across 11 CT foundation models on six biomarker tasks, and additionally evaluates dense segmentation (AMOS-CT, KiTS23, LiTS, WORD) and zero-shot text-to-image retrieval (CT-RATE, Merlin), covering local, dense, and semantic levels of representation quality.

Strong empirical results in several regimes: best frozen-embedding kNN performance on 4/6 biomarker tasks with narrow confidence intervals (Fig. 3), best performance among transformer-based segmenters and competitive with nnU-Net despite an encoder-only head (Table 1), and large retrieval gains over CT-CLIP and general-domain CLIP models (Table 2), plus best Impressions and Full-Report retrieval on Merlin.

Fully open training corpus (229,619 image series from public datasets, with per-dataset filtering documented in Table 4 and Section A), released code/model, and detailed hyperparameters (Tables 5-6) and hardware description, which supports reproducibility and community reuse.

Honest reporting in places: the authors disclose that tuning was done on KiTS23 fold-0 and exclude that fold, report limitations (thoracic skew of the corpus, report noise, smooth low-resolution segmentation masks), and show ablations (Table 7) rather than hiding negative comparisons.

The two-stage local/global ViT design with anisotropic 3D tokenization, 3D RoPE, and window-then-scan attention is a sensible, well-motivated engineering solution to token scaling in volumetric transformers, and the equations are specified precisely enough to reimplement.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the approach is essentially DINOv3-style SSL plus SigLIP VLA on a windowed 3D ViT with 3D RoPE and EoMT-derived segmentation; each component is adapted from prior work, and the paper offers no ablation isolating the claimed benefit of the two-stage SSL-then-VLA pipeline for representation quality (only a small crop-size/initialization ablation on KiTS23 fold-0).

Key quantitative evidence is relegated to figures: the main biomarker comparison (Fig. 1) and the per-model statistics (Fig. 3) are radar/bar plots without a numeric table, making precise margins between SPECTRE and, e.g., FMCIB or CT-FM difficult to verify; some results also lack confidence-interval reporting in the main text.

Claims are somewhat overstated relative to the evidence: the abstract asserts SPECTRE 'consistently outperforms prior CT foundation models in both zero-shot and fine-tuned settings,' yet it is below SOTA on 2/6 biomarker tasks, below Merlin on Findings retrieval (55.5 vs 77.6 Recall@1 at N=32), and below nnU-Net ResEnc L on segmentation; 'zero-shot' framing is also loose given LoRA-tuned text encoders and model-selection choices.

Baseline comparability concerns: the doubling of field of view for NSCLC-Radiogenomics and Colorectal-Liver-Metastases is applied to SPECTRE, and segmentation baselines are taken from prior papers under slightly different tuning regimes (fold-0 tuning for some baselines), which weakens the fairness of the cross-model claims.

The retrieval evaluation omits some potentially informative baselines and the language side (Qwen3-0.6B + LoRA, LLM-rewritten reports via Gemini 2 Flash) introduces a data- and model-dependent confound whose contribution to retrieval gains is not disentangled from the vision encoder quality.

Ablation coverage is thin relative to the design space: no experiments on the choice of window count G, the pooling/concatenation scheme in Eq. 6, alternative patch sizes, or the effect of omitting the Gram loss, leaving the central architectural decisions empirically unsubstantiated.

strengths: Comprehensive, standardized evaluation across three distinct task families: frozen-embedding biomarker kNN classification on the TumorImagingBench protocol (11 models, 6 datasets), semantic segmentation on the Isensee-recommended CT suite (AMOS-CT, KiTS23, LiTS, WORD) integrated into nnU-Net, and zero-shot text-to-image retrieval on CT-RATE and Merlin. This breadth is uncommon and well executed.

Strong empirical results: best performance on 4/6 biomarker benchmarks with narrow confidence intervals (Fig. 3), competitive with or better than specialized transformer segmentors despite an encoder-only head (Table 1), and substantial retrieval gains over CT-CLIP (Table 2) and over Merlin on Impressions retrieval (Table 3).

Fully open, reproducible contribution: model, training code, and recipes released; pretraining restricted to public datasets; the supplementary provides substantial detail on data curation (per-dataset filtering criteria, e.g., Tukey-rule head-CT exclusion for CT-RATE), preprocessing, hyperparameters (Tables 5-6), and hardware, which is unusually thorough for a foundation model paper.

Principled handling of CT-specific challenges: anisotropic patching aligned with voxel geometry, 3D RoPE with box jittering for resolution/FOV robustness, and a local/global two-stage attention design that makes scan-level attention tractable (formalized cost analysis in Eq. 4).

Honest reporting: the paper acknowledges where it does not reach SOTA (2/6 biomarker tasks, Findings retrieval), the thoracic skew of the corpus, and limitations of the 1/4-resolution segmentation masks; the KiTS23 fold-0 tuning contamination is explicitly handled by excluding that fold.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the method is largely a careful adaptation of existing recipes (DINOv3/iBOT/KoLeo, SigLIP, 3D RoPE, EoMT-style encoder segmentation) to volumetric CT. The local/global two-stage ViT and windowed [cls]-token aggregation are sensible but incremental, and the paper does not include ablations isolating these core architectural choices (e.g., number of windows G, window size, two-stage vs. joint pretraining).

The contribution of the VLA stage is not well quantified on the headline results. The SSL-vs-VLA ablation (Table 7) exists only for segmentation and shows the gap nearly vanishes at larger crop sizes (0.871 vs 0.871); there is no analogous ablation for the biomarker or retrieval benchmarks, making it hard to attribute the reported gains to the two-stage pipeline versus scale and data curation alone.

Baseline comparisons have asymmetries: several segmentation numbers are imported from other papers under slightly different tuning regimes, and the CT-RATE retrieval comparison includes only CT-CLIP as a CT-specific baseline while stronger recent VLA models are discussed but not evaluated.

Claims occasionally outrun evidence: 'consistently outperforms prior CT foundation models' holds on only 4/6 biomarker tasks, and the paper itself notes performance is weaker on abdominal tasks, plausibly due to the corpus being ~70% chest CT (NLST alone is 132,985 of 229,619 series).

Some important methodological details are deferred to the supplementary (pretraining data pipeline, hardware, training recipe), so the main text alone does not fully support reproducibility, and the retrieval section's use of LLM-generated report paraphrases (Gemini 2 Flash) introduces a data-augmentation dependence that is not ablated.

The finding that VLA initialization only helps at small crop sizes (Table 7) is interesting but unexplored; it raises questions about whether the expensive second pretraining stage provides value at inference scales that matter.

strengths: Large-scale, fully open foundation model: trained on ~230k CT series from publicly available datasets (Tab. 4) with code, weights, and recipes promised for release — a meaningful contribution to reproducibility in medical imaging.

Comprehensive evaluation across three distinct task families: frozen-embedding kNN biomarker classification under the standardized TumorImagingBench protocol (Pai et al.), semantic segmentation within nnU-Net with a rigorous 5-fold cross-validation protocol, and zero-shot text-to-image retrieval on CT-RATE and Merlin.

Strong empirical results: best performance on 4/6 biomarker benchmarks (Fig. 1, Fig. 3 with 95% CIs), substantial retrieval improvements over CT-CLIP on CT-RATE (e.g., R@100: 59.9 vs 28.8), and competitive segmentation against dedicated transformer architectures (Tab. 1) as well as encoder-only results on TotalSegmentator benchmarks (Tab. 9).

Honest self-assessment: the discussion clearly identifies limitations (thoracic-skewed corpus, report noise, smoothed fine structures at 1/4 resolution), and the supplementary decoder ablation (Tab. 10) candidly shows the SEoMT encoder-only design understates small-lesion performance.

The two-stage SSL (DINOv3-style) then VLA (SigLIP) pipeline with LLM-based report paraphrasing is a well-motivated design for the noisy many-to-many image-text structure of radiology, and the ablations on optimizer, crop size, SSL vs VLA initialization, and report dropout provide useful engineering insights.
Detailed supplementary material (data curation, preprocessing, hyperparameters, hardware) supports reproducibility of a complex training pipeline.
weaknesses: Main-paper presentation of the headline biomarker results is weak: quantitative results are relegated to a radar plot (Fig. 1) and a bar chart (Fig. 3) without numeric tables or AUC values in the main text, making precise comparison with prior work difficult for the reader.

The title and abstract emphasize 'scaling', but no scaling analysis is presented: the model is modest in size (339M + 58M parameters, Tab. 6) and there are no scaling curves (model, data, or compute) to support scaling claims.

Novelty is primarily integration and adaptation of existing techniques (DINOv3, iBOT, KoLeo, SigLIP, RoPE, EoMT) to 3D CT rather than fundamentally new methods; the architecture is reasonable but incremental relative to prior 3D transformer work (e.g., Primus).

Segmentation gains over the strongest transformer baseline are marginal (e.g., KiTS23: 86.64 vs Primus-M 86.13; LiTS: 80.14 vs 79.90) and likely within cross-fold variance; furthermore, baseline numbers are taken from Wald et al. under a different tuning setup (fold-0 excluded for baselines on KiTS23 and LiTS), which complicates direct comparability despite the stated fairness motivation.

On Merlin retrieval, SPECTRE loses clearly to the region-specialized Merlin model on the Findings section (e.g., R@1 at N=128: 33.0 vs 59.4), so the cross-modal alignment claim holds mainly for Impressions and combined reports; the paper does not fully reconcile this asymmetry.

Potential data-advantage confound: SPECTRE pretrains on 229k series including NLST (133k), considerably more data than several compared models (e.g., FMCIB ~11.5k patches, Merlin ~15k); the contribution of architecture vs. corpus scale is not disentangled, and no compute-matched or data-matched baselines are provided.

Some methodological details are under-specified in the main paper, e.g., how the full resampled volume (up to 512×512×384) is partitioned into G=36 windows at inference and how scan-level embeddings are formed for the kNN benchmark, which matters for reproducing the reported results.

The LLM-based report rewriting (Gemini 2 Flash) introduces synthetic supervision whose effect is only indirectly analyzed; a direct ablation of paraphrasing on downstream retrieval/classification would strengthen the VLA claims.

strengths: Comprehensive, carefully standardized evaluation: the paper adopts the TumorImagingBench protocol of Pai et al. uniformly across 11 foundation models for biomarker prediction (Fig. 1/Fig. 3 with 95% CIs), uses an nnU-Net-integrated encoder-only segmentation probe across six datasets (Tabs. 1, 9, 10), and evaluates zero-shot retrieval on two benchmarks (Tabs. 2, 3). This breadth and protocol discipline is above average for foundation-model papers.

Fully open pretraining: the model is trained exclusively on ~230k publicly available CT series (Tab. 4) with detailed dataset curation, filtering, and preprocessing recipes in the supplement, and the model, code, and nnU-Net integration are stated to be publicly released, which is a genuine community contribution.

The two-stage DINOv3-style SSL + SigLIP VLA pipeline is sensibly adapted to 3D (e.g., increased masking ratio justified by 3D neighborhood density, LLM-based report paraphrasing following LaCLIP, EHR code handling), and the supplementary ablations (Tabs. 8, 10; Fig. 8) probe optimizer, crop size, SSL vs. VLA initialization, decoder choice, and report corruption robustness.

Honest treatment of limitations: the paper explicitly reports the two biomarker tasks where it does not achieve SOTA, acknowledges the thoracic skew of the corpus, and the decoder ablation (Tab. 10) transparently shows a stronger UNETR decoder improves small-lesion performance over the encoder-only SEoMT.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty. The architecture and objectives are largely an assembly of existing components: DINO/iBOT/KoLeo (DINOv2/v3 recipe), SigLIP, 3D RoPE, windowed local attention with a global aggregator, and EoMT-style query segmentation. The paper itself frames the contribution as 'minimal adaptations' of a plain ViT; no new objective, architectural principle, or analysis is introduced, so the contribution rests heavily on scale and the released artifact.

Headline empirical wins are mixed rather than dominant. SPECTRE wins 4/6 biomarker tasks but loses NSCLC-Radiogenomics and Colorectal-Liver-Metastases (with wide CIs on the two tasks where it loses); in segmentation it reaches 86.64 on KiTS23 vs. Primus-M's 86.13 and remains below nnU-Net ResEnc L (88.06); on Merlin Findings retrieval it is clearly behind Merlin (55.5 vs. 77.6 R@1 at N=32). The abstract's 'consistently outperforms prior CT foundation models' overstates this pattern.

Key design decisions are under-justified. The unusual embedding dimension d=1080, the 65,536 prototypes, G=36 windows, and the two-stage (vs. joint) training schedule are asserted rather than ablated; the 'compression factor 2048/1080 ≈ 1.8962' (Sec. 3.1) is presented as if meaningful but is not. There is no FLOPs/memory comparison substantiating the efficiency claims of Sec. 3, and Eq. 4 mislabels the local-window cost as 'Costglobal'.

Pretraining corpus composition undermines the 'general-purpose' framing: 132,985 of 229,619 series (58%) come from NLST chest screening, and the authors themselves attribute weaker abdominal performance to this skew (Sec. 6). The claims of broad anatomical generality are therefore not well supported by the data distribution.

Reproducibility details have gaps: footnote 1 reads 'Code available at:' with no URL; the Gemini 2 Flash paraphrasing step introduces a closed, non-reproducible data-processing component into the pretraining pipeline; and some downstream baseline numbers are inherited from Wald et al. rather than re-run, which the paper does flag but which weakens strict comparability.

Presentation issues: Fig. 1's radar plot is difficult to read with 11 overlapping models; there are typos ('hyperperameters', 'This approach does predict masks at 1/4'), and the related-work positioning (Sec. 2.2) is largely descriptive rather than analytically differentiating SPECTRE from CT-FM and Primus, its closest competitors.

strengths: Comprehensive and well-standardized empirical evaluation: the paper assesses SPECTRE across three distinct task families (frozen-embedding biomarker classification via the standardized TumorImagingBench protocol of Pai et al., dense semantic segmentation within nnU-Net, and zero-shot text-to-image retrieval on CT-RATE and Merlin), comparing against 11 CT foundation models under harmonized preprocessing, which makes the comparisons meaningful rather than cherry-picked.

Solid and competitive empirical results: best performance on 4/6 biomarker tasks with narrow confidence intervals on the winning tasks, segmentation results (86.64 KiTS23 / 80.14 LiTS / 83.31 WORD) that surpass all other transformer baselines and approach nnU-Net ResEnc L without decoder-heavy design, and substantially improved retrieval over CT-CLIP on CT-RATE (e.g., 17.5 vs 2.9 R@5).

Transparent, unusually honest experimental hygiene: tuning on KiTS23 fold-0 is explicitly excluded from final results; the supplementary includes decoder ablations (Linear/SEoMT/UNETR) showing the encoder-only protocol may understate small-lesion performance, robustness analyses (voxel spacing, token/span dropout, report length), and clear limitation discussion (thoracic skew, report noise, smooth segmentation outputs).

Valuable open-science contribution: the model, training code, and pretraining recipes are released, and the corpus is built exclusively from openly available data (229,619 series from NLST, CT-RATE, INSPECT, Merlin, etc.), lowering the barrier for the community and demonstrating that strong 3D CT representations do not require private data.

Well-motivated engineering framing: the local/global two-stage ViT with 3D RoPE, anisotropic tokenization, and windowed-then-global attention directly addresses the token-scaling and anisotropy issues of volumetric CT, and the SigLIP choice is well justified for noisy, many-to-many report supervision.
Rich supplementary material (preprocessing, hyperparameters, additional TotalSegmentator benchmarks, ablations on optimizer, crop size, and SSL vs VLA initialization) supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the method is essentially a careful adaptation of existing components (DINOv3 self-distillation, iBOT/KoLeo, SigLIP, 3D RoPE, EoMT-style segmentation) to the volumetric domain. The architectural novelty (windowed local ViT + small global aggregation ViT) is sensible but incremental relative to prior 3D transformer designs such as Primus and CT-FM.

The title emphasizes 'Scaling', but no scaling analysis is provided: there are no experiments varying pretraining data size, model size, or compute, and no evidence on how performance scales with corpus or architecture size, which weakens the central framing of the paper.

Key biomarker results appear only in a radar plot (Fig. 1) and a bar chart with confidence intervals (Fig. 3) rather than in a numeric table, making precise comparison and verification difficult; additionally, the radar plot on page 1 appears to mislabel an axis (duplicate NSCLC-Radiomics label), which should be corrected.

Some design choices are under-justified or not ablated: the embedding dimension d=1080 and its 'effective compression factor of 1.8962' rationale is idiosyncratic; the number of windows (G=36), masking ratio range, omission of the DINOv3 Gram loss, and the local/global decomposition are asserted rather than ablated, so the contribution of each architectural decision to the reported gains is unclear.

State-of-the-art is not reached on several benchmarks: two of six biomarker tasks are lost, LiTS and WORD segmentation trail nnU-Net ResEnc L, and Merlin remains clearly better on Findings-based retrieval; the paper handles this honestly, but overall the evidence supports 'competitive' rather than 'consistently outperforms' as the abstract implies.

Reliance on a closed LLM (Gemini 2 Flash) for report paraphrasing introduces an unreproducible component into the VLA pipeline, and no ablation quantifies the benefit of LLM-based rewriting versus raw reports despite the Discussion attributing retrieval robustness partly to these rewrites.

Heavy compute footprint (24 B200 GPUs) with limited discussion of efficiency relative to competing models, and the segmentation claim of 4 datasets in Table 1 is actually 3 (KiTS23, LiTS, WORD), which is a presentation inconsistency.
